title: 'Flock Flocked up'

reading.body:
This is a false-positive identification failure at the front end of a policing workflow. An automated licence plate reader flagged a plate as stolen when it was not, and the misread was passed to officers as a reason to stop a vehicle. The mismatch was visible in the system's own output: the camera image was of a Chevy Malibu, while the plate was on a red Dodge Ram pickup. The failure occurred before any human contact, at the point where a machine-generated alert was treated as sufficient grounds for an armed stop.

Catching it would have required a comparison of the flagged plate against the vehicle it was attached to, either by the system or by a person reviewing the alert before it reached the street. The facts do not show that any such check took place. The department's own K-9 policy called for handlers to weigh the severity of the crime, any immediate threat, and whether a suspect was resisting or hiding before deploying a dog, which places a second decision point after the stop had already begun.

What is not established is whether the misread was a known limitation of the camera system, whether officers were told the alert was unverified, or whether the department's finding of no wrongdoing in the K-9 use settles any question about the stop itself. The reports describe an investigation and dropped charges, not a determination of fault.

reports.title: Body cam of TPD officers releasing K-9 on man during traffic stop
Man speaks out after police release K-9 on him during traffic stop: 'Traumatized'
TPD investigation finds no wrongdoing in use of K-9 on man during traffic stop
Charges dropped against man Toledo Police released K-9 on during traffic stop, lawyer says

summary:
Toledo Police released body camera video showing officers using a K-9 on a driver during a traffic stop. The stop began after a FLOCK camera wrongly flagged a stolen license plate. The camera image belonged to a Chevy Malibu, but the plate was seen on a red Dodge Ram pickup. Officers stopped driver Brandon Upchurch with guns drawn and ordered him out. He raised his hands, asked why he was stopped, and was arrested, then charged with resisting arrest and obstruction. He received medical attention at the scene.

Officers later learned the plate information was a misread and not stolen. Police said they thought Upchurch might flee and did not know if he or a passenger had weapons. The department's K-9 policy says handlers should weigh the crime's severity, any immediate threat, and whether a suspect is resisting or hiding before deploying a dog. Multiple officers are under investigation, and the article does not say what happens next.
